hints: Look for two particles that are doing exactly the same thing - same displacement from equilibrium and moving in the same direction. On the sine curve below, where does the pattern exactly repeat?
walkthrough:
**What one wavelength means for particles**
Think of wavelength $\lambda$ as the repeat distance. Two particles one $\lambda$ apart are in phase. They have the same displacement and the same velocity at the same instant.

**Spot the repeat on Fig. 4.1**
The lower graph is displacement against distance. It repeats after one full sine wave. The left-most particle is at zero displacement moving right, and particle Y is also at zero displacement moving right. Count the particles between them and you find seven in between. Those two are exactly one $\lambda$ apart. Any other pair with the same separation also works.
Final answer: Circle any two particles separated by one complete cycle, e.g. the left-most particle and particle Y, with seven uncircled particles between them.

hints: Picture the whole sine pattern sliding sideways as time passes. Which way does a progressive wave travelling left to right move its pattern in a short time?
In one full period T the pattern moves by one full wavelength. So how far does it shift in only T/4?
Check what happens at distance zero: the original curve starts at 0 going up, but after the shift the new curve must start below zero. Keep the height and length of the waves the same.
walkthrough:
**Slide the pattern to the right**
You have a progressive wave moving left to right. As time goes forward the displacement-distance curve keeps its shape but slides to the right. It does not grow or shrink if there is no damping.

**How far in T/4**
In time $T$ the wave travels one wavelength $\lambda$. So in time $$ \Delta t = T/4 $$ it travels $$ \Delta x = \frac{\lambda}{4} $$ to the right. Draw the same sine wave, same peak height and same spacing, but moved right by a quarter of a cycle.

**Check the start**
At distance $=0$ the old curve was at $0$ and rising. After moving right by $\lambda/4$, the value at $0$ is now what used to be $\lambda/4$ to the left, which is a trough value. So your new curve starts at negative displacement with the same magnitude as the old amplitude, then rises through zero. That constant phase shift all along keeps the wavelength unchanged.
Final answer: Sine curve of same amplitude and same wavelength shifted to the right by $\lambda/4$, starting at negative displacement at distance zero.

hints: Focus on particle Z on the new shifted curve from (a)(ii). Is Z now on a part of the curve where displacement is about to become more positive or more negative as the wave keeps moving right?
walkthrough:
**Read motion from the shifted curve**
For a longitudinal wave, positive displacement means displacement to the right of equilibrium. At time $t_0 + T/4$ particle Z sits on a section of the shifted sine curve where the next part of the wave arriving from the left will push its displacement to more positive values. Increasing positive displacement means moving to the right.

**Longitudinal picture**
You can also think of compressions and rarefactions moving right. Z is just to the right of a compression at $t_0$. A quarter period later the compression has moved right past Z, so Z is pulled back to the right as the compression passes.
Final answer: To the right / rightwards.

hints: Look carefully at points X and Y on the displacement graph. X is at a zero crossing going down and Y is at the next zero crossing going up. What fraction of a full wavelength is that separation?
Once you have the true wavelength, think about which universal wave relation links speed with the frequency and wavelength you now know.
Remember to convert $16\text{ kHz}$ to Hz before multiplying, and keep your distance in metres to get speed in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
**Get wavelength from XY**
X is at displacement $0$ falling to negative, Y is at the next displacement $0$ rising to positive. That is half a cycle from one zero slope to the opposite zero slope. So $$ XY = \frac{\lambda}{2} $$ Hence $$ \lambda = 2 \times 0.19 = 0.38\text{ m} $$

**Apply the wave equation**
For any progressive wave $$ v = f\lambda $$ Frequency is $$ f = 16\text{ kHz} = 16 \times 10^3\text{ Hz} $$

**Calculate speed**
$$ v = (16 \times 10^3) \times 0.38 $$ $$ v = 6080\text{ m s}^{-1} \approx 6.1 \times 10^3\text{ m s}^{-1} $$ to 2 s.f. This very high speed is typical for sound in a solid.
Final answer: $\lambda = 2 \times 0.19 = 0.38\text{ m}$, $v = f\lambda = (16 \times 10^3) \times 0.38 = 6.1 \times 10^3\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

hints: Intensity tells you about power per unit area carried by the wave. If frequency stays the same but the vibrations get smaller, how does that energy depend on amplitude - linearly or by a power law?
If amplitude becomes $1/2$ of the original, work out what happens when you square that factor and apply it to $I_0$.
walkthrough:
**Recall the intensity law**
For a wave of constant frequency in the same medium, intensity is proportional to the square of amplitude: $$ I \propto A^2 $$ This is because wave energy is proportional to (amplitude)$^2$, like elastic potential energy $\propto x^2$.

**Apply the halving**
New amplitude $A = A_0/2$. So $$ \frac{I}{I_0} = \left(\frac{A}{A_0}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{4} $$ Hence $$ I = 0.25 I_0 $$ Halving amplitude quarters the intensity.
Final answer: $I \propto A^2$, so $I = (1/2)^2 I_0 = 0.25 I_0$.

hints: Two opposite waves will only make a stable standing pattern with fixed nodes if their basic timing matches. What wave property must be identical so peaks keep meeting peaks in the same places?
walkthrough:
**Why matching timing matters**
A stationary wave forms by superposition of two progressive waves travelling in opposite directions. To keep nodes fixed in space, the two waves must stay in step with each other all the time. That needs the same frequency, and therefore the same wavelength and period in the same medium. Ideally they also have similar amplitude for clear nodes.
Final answer: The two waves must have the same frequency (same wavelength / period).

hints: Think about energy: a progressive wave carries energy along as it travels, but what happens to net energy flow when two equal opposite waves trap the energy between fixed points?

Think about what different points along the medium do: in a travelling wave every particle vibrates with the same size, but in a standing pattern some points never move at all. What are those points called and how does phase differ?
walkthrough:
**Energy and shape**
A progressive wave propagates energy in its direction of travel, and its profile moves along. A stationary wave stores energy in one place, with no net transfer, and its envelope stays fixed with permanent nodes where displacement is always zero and antinodes where it is maximum.

**Amplitude and phase**
In a progressive wave all particles vibrate with the same amplitude, and phase changes smoothly with distance so neighbours are slightly out of phase. In a stationary wave amplitude depends on position, zero at nodes and maximum at antinodes, and all particles between two adjacent nodes vibrate in phase with each other.

Final answer: Any two of: stationary wave has nodes/antinodes whereas progressive does not; stationary wave does not transfer net energy whereas progressive does; amplitude varies with position for stationary (maximum at antinodes, zero at nodes) whereas amplitude is same for all particles for progressive; adjacent particles between nodes are in phase for stationary whereas adjacent particles have a phase difference for progressive.
